title: China and India Want Much the Same Things From South Asia
gist: Chatham House's Chietigj Bajpaee argues that after the 2025-26 China-India reset, the two powers share regional interests in South Asia (water, development, failed states) and should coordinate there, since most South Asian states hedge between them and Western attention has receded.

insights.claim: China-India relations have partially normalized since the 2020 border clashes, with Xi's first India visit in almost seven years at the September BRICS summit, resumed direct flights, relaxed visa and investment restrictions, an eight-point border consensus in August, and trade resuming along three border passes after six years.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: De-escalation lowers tail risk on the border and supports bilateral trade and investment recovery.
insights.locator: Last month's BRICS summit marked the pinnacle

insights.claim: The reset predates Trump's second term but accelerated under it, as both China and India are targets of his tariffs and sanctions over Russian energy purchases, while each independently keeps relations with Washington stable.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: US pressure is pushing Beijing and New Delhi toward tactical alignment; US-India trade deal progress remains a swing factor.

insights.claim: The BRICS New Delhi Declaration of 140 points criticized unilateral coercive measures and called for a predictable, rules-based multilateral trading system, with several references to the Trump administration's disruptive policies.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: BRICS messaging is increasingly framed against US trade unilateralism.

insights.claim: China has become a leading trade, investment and defense partner for most South Asian countries, motivated by a stable periphery, markets, and alternate trade routes to ease the Malacca Dilemma, while India views this as strategic encirclement but has abandoned the idea of South Asia as its exclusive sphere.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Chinese port and infrastructure presence in South Asia is entrenched; India's response is partnership with Japan and others.

insights.claim: China has built India-excluding initiatives, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, trilaterals with Bangladesh-Pakistan and Afghanistan-Pakistan, the Colombo International Container Terminal and the Mongla Port modernization in Bangladesh.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Chinese-operated ports in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are tracked as strategic assets.

insights.claim: SAARC has not held a summit since 2014 because of India-Pakistan tensions, prompting some to consider a South Asian regional architecture without India.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Absence of a regional forum leaves space for China-led formats.

insights.claim: Most South Asian states pursue multialignment and try to exploit Sino-Indian rivalry for concessions, though concerns about Chinese opaque lending such as Sri Lanka's Hambantota project limit the benefit.

insights.so_what: Smaller states will not choose sides, so expect competing project offers.

insights.claim: China should be included in multilateral water arrangements because most major South Asian rivers originate there, given China's construction of the world's largest hydropower project on the Brahmaputra/Yarlung Tsangpo, and the Indus Waters Treaty is in abeyance while the Ganga Water Treaty expires in December.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Water treaty lapses are a flashpoint to watch in December.

insights.claim: Nepal's prime minister Balendra Shah proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism with China and India after the glacial-collapse floods, while the two powers delivered aid in parallel rather than in coordination.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Illustrates low-cost avenue for China-India coordination.

insights.claim: China and India both pursue separate and sometimes opposed factional strategies in near-failed states Afghanistan and Myanmar, though both seek a stable periphery and economic opportunities.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: A joint approach is argued but not yet present; instability there persists.

insights.claim: South Asia has lost strategic significance in the West since the 2021 US/NATO Afghanistan withdrawal and aid cutbacks, while more than 70 percent of India's 2026-27 foreign aid budget goes to South Asia.
insights.speaker: Chietigj Bajpaee
insights.so_what: Western retreat leaves China and India as principal external financiers of the region.
